title: Beamed-energy launch of a useful payload into orbit

concept.text: Concept synthesis: a ground- or space-based laser or microwave transmitter supplies most of the energy needed to propel a vehicle carrying a useful payload into Earth orbit. The vehicle receives the beam and converts its energy into propulsion. The defining achievement is sustained propulsion through enough of the ascent to accomplish orbital insertion, rather than simply receiving power or making a short flight.

Architectural clarification: the remote beam is an energy supply, while the propulsion mechanism determines how that energy produces thrust. A vehicle could still need substantial reaction mass, onboard energy, and propulsion equipment. Moving the principal energy source off the vehicle does not specify how much propellant it carries. Likewise, delivering electricity to a stationary photovoltaic receiver demonstrates power transfer, not orbital launch; DARPA's POWER experiment illustrates that distinction.

significance.text: Conditional architectural significance: successful orbital launch powered predominantly by a remote beam would separate the vehicle from its principal energy source. Chemical rockets carry propellants whose stored chemical energy powers ascent; a beamed-energy vehicle could receive its principal propulsion energy from external infrastructure. This would establish a distinct launch architecture and could reduce the need to carry an onboard energy supply.

Limits of that inference: leaving the power plant behind does not establish that the vehicle can dispense with most of its propellant, that electricity represents the entire energy cost, or that launch becomes inexpensive. Reaction-mass requirements, propulsion hardware, beam-generation efficiency, atmospheric losses, conversion losses, infrastructure, and operating demands depend on the design. A beam supplying a majority of ascent energy establishes an energy-source relationship, not a particular mass saving or economic outcome.

Conditional downstream possibilities: a successful kilogram-class orbital demonstration could motivate larger launch systems, human transport, point-to-point Earth transport, or networks of beam stations. Those capabilities would require additional development in transmitted power, tracking coverage, vehicle thermal protection, reliability, and operations. They would not follow automatically from the first useful-payload launch.

missing_breakthrough.text: Engineering synthesis: the unsolved capability targeted by this entry is an integrated system that couples remote electromagnetic energy into a moving vehicle strongly enough, and for long enough, to place a useful payload in orbit. Short flights and laboratory energy-coupling experiments can establish components of that capability, but do not establish the energy delivery, trajectory, or sustained operation needed for orbital insertion. The supplied evidence does not establish the latest worldwide development status.

Engineering synthesis: relevant barriers include propagating the beam through the atmosphere, keeping it aligned with a rapidly moving receiver, converting the received energy into adequate thrust, and maintaining vehicle integrity under concentrated heating. The system must also accommodate changing range, geometry, and atmospheric conditions during ascent. These are requirements inferred from the architecture; the supplied propulsion evidence does not establish their relative difficulty, an exhaustive barrier list, or demonstrated solutions.

The demonstrated separation between remote power reception and propulsion remains important. DARPA's ground experiment converted laser energy into electricity using a mirror and photovoltaic cells. Such reception can inform enabling technology, but it does not establish a flightworthy propulsion system, moving-target beam coupling, or orbital energy delivery.

current_state.text: The supplied research attributes a historical Lightcraft flight to AIAA paper 2001-3798, World Record Flights of Beam-Riding Rocket Lightcraft: on 2 October 2000 at White Sands, a 12.2 cm diameter, 50.6 g vehicle reportedly reached 71 m using a 10 kW pulsed carbon-dioxide laser. These numerical details are preserved as an attributed historical report. Although the research says an open copy was inspected in an earlier pass, the supplied evidence review had no retained paper text with which to verify them. That access limitation leaves the details unverified here; it is not evidence that the flight report is false.

On 16 May 2025, DARPA reported that its POWER program delivered more than 800 watts during a 30-second transmission from a laser 8.6 km away in New Mexico. A parabolic mirror directed the beam onto dozens of photovoltaic cells, producing usable electricity; the team used some of the transferred energy to make popcorn. Both transmitter and receiver were on the ground. This was a power-transfer demonstration, not a vehicle-propulsion demonstration. The supplied review describes the retained article as complete, untruncated, and free of extraction issues.

Evidence boundary as of 1 November 2026: the supplied material does not establish whether the 71 m Lightcraft flight remains the published free-flight altitude record, or whether any beamed-energy payload has subsequently reached space or orbit. No supplied freshness search resolves those questions. The material therefore supports a dated power-transfer achievement and an attributed historical propulsion report, while leaving present record-holder and worldwide nonachievement claims open. It does not establish completion of the orbital-launch capability.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: place a payload of at least 1 kg into Earth orbit, with payload mass and orbital parameters independently measured. Specify the required orbital lifetime before the test so that 'stable orbit' has an operational meaning. The kilogram threshold and lifetime requirement are proposed criteria for this record, not established standards or documented goals of the cited DARPA program.
completion_criteria.label: Independently verified Earth orbit for at least 1 kg

completion_criteria.text: Proposed energy accounting: define the ascent interval, system boundary, and energy metric before launch, then use metering and a documented energy balance to show that the remote electromagnetic beam supplies more than half of ascent energy within that boundary. Measure beam energy delivered to the vehicle and onboard energy contributions, and account explicitly for conversion losses and stored energy. Distinguish received beam energy from energy actually contributing to propulsion; a large amount of unused beam energy should not establish predominance. Onboard energy and propellant may support steering or circularization, provided their treatment is explicit and the majority-energy criterion is met.
completion_criteria.label: Beam supplies more than half of accounted ascent propulsion energy

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: make trajectory measurements, energy-accounting methods, calibration information, and uncertainty estimates available for independent assessment, and repeat the launch sufficiently to establish reproducibility. Report payload, atmospheric conditions, beam range, tracking coverage, thermal limits, and infrastructure used. Such tests would establish capability over the demonstrated operating envelope; they would not establish all-weather operation, arbitrary payload scaling, economical service, or suitability for people.
completion_criteria.label: Reproducible launches with independently assessable measurements and reported operating boundaries

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis — ROC-03, A directed-energy lightsail accelerated to a substantial fraction of light speed, shares the separation of vehicle and remote energy source, along with beam-pointing and propagation challenges. Its defining mechanism is photon momentum acting on a sail, and its target is a substantial fraction of light speed. ROC-02 instead concerns useful-payload orbital launch and leaves the beam-to-thrust mechanism open; success in either entry would not by itself complete the other.

Roster-based synthesis — ROC-01, Sustained air-breathing combined-cycle flight to orbital speed, also seeks a different route to orbital launch, but centers on atmospheric operation and propulsion-mode integration. ROC-02 centers on remote energy delivery. A hybrid could combine aspects of both, while still needing to demonstrate each entry's defining capability.

Roster-based synthesis — ROC-04, Open-cycle gas-core nuclear rocket with high thrust and multi-thousand-second specific impulse, and ROC-05, Fission-fragment rocket with direct conversion of fragment momentum into thrust, concern distinct nuclear propulsion mechanisms. Their central breakthroughs concern producing thrust from nuclear processes, whereas ROC-02 concerns delivering propulsion energy remotely. Beam generation could draw on different energy sources without making the receiving vehicle either of those nuclear rocket types.

Roster-based synthesis — ROC-06, A plasma-magnet sail that takes useful delta-v from the solar wind, and ROC-07, An operational momentum-exchange tether that moves payloads between orbits, also involve interaction with something external to the payload vehicle. The plasma-magnet sail uses the solar wind; the tether exchanges momentum mechanically. Neither is a remote electromagnetic energy beam supplying most of a launch ascent, and neither entry's stated goal is the same orbital-launch demonstration.

Roster-based synthesis — ROC-08, Industrial-scale production and loading of rocket propellant off Earth, addresses propellant supply rather than remote propulsion energy. It could complement beamed-energy systems that still consume reaction mass. Keeping the entries distinct preserves the difference between obtaining propellant and providing the energy that drives propulsion.

Architectural synthesis: stationary photovoltaic power reception is an enabling technology related to ROC-02, as the DARPA result illustrates. Evacuated-tube and lunar electromagnetic launchers are separate architectures that accelerate vehicles through launcher infrastructure rather than sustained reception of a remote beam. The research associates ROC-02 with a historical ground-based beamed-propulsion item, but that item's exact wording was not independently supplied, so its precise correspondence remains unverified.

change_log.change: Preserved ROC-02's identity and orbital-launch target while explaining the distinction between remote energy supply, propulsion mechanism, and reaction mass.
change_log.reason: The concept remains coherent despite incomplete propulsion evidence; moving an energy source off the vehicle does not determine propellant requirements.

change_log.change: Retained the historical Lightcraft date, dimensions, mass, altitude, location, and laser power as an attributed report with an explicit verification limitation.
change_log.reason: The research contains useful quantitative detail, but the validated review had no retained paper text. Missing evidence does not establish that the report is false.

change_log.change: Removed categorical assertions that the Lightcraft flight remains the altitude record and that no beamed-energy payload has reached space.
change_log.reason: The supplied material contains no freshness search sufficient to establish either present-day assertion.

change_log.change: Integrated DARPA's dated power, duration, distance, receiver mechanism, ground configuration, and popcorn demonstration.
change_log.reason: The retained article supports these details and makes clear why the result demonstrates power transfer rather than propulsion.

change_log.change: Qualified claims about propellant elimination, electricity-only energy cost, and launch economics, while preserving conditional architectural significance and downstream possibilities.
change_log.reason: Those outcomes depend on propulsion design, reaction mass, losses, infrastructure, and operations; they do not follow from predominantly remote ascent energy.

change_log.change: Expanded the proposed kilogram-class orbital test with independent measurements, a specified orbital lifetime, explicit energy accounting, reproducibility, and operating-envelope reporting.
change_log.reason: The original terms 'most of the energy' and 'stable orbit' need operational definitions. These refinements remain proposals rather than source-established standards.

change_log.change: Explained relationships to every other supplied roster entry and preserved the distinction from stationary power reception and track- or tube-based launchers.
change_log.reason: Shared enabling technologies and possible combinations do not make the entries interchangeable.

unresolved_issues: The Lightcraft paper's identity and numerical flight details remain unverified from retained document content; the earlier research's claimed inspection cannot substitute for the missing artifact.
The present laser-propelled free-flight altitude record and the worldwide status of beamed-energy launches to space or orbit remain unresolved as of 1 November 2026.
The supplied sources do not establish a current orbital-propulsion program, its technical maturity, or the relative severity of the inferred engineering barriers.

A demonstration protocol still needs a precise energy metric and measurement method that distinguish beam energy received, conversion losses, and energy contributing to ascent, together with uncertainty treatment.
The required orbital lifetime, repetition count, and practical operating envelope remain choices for a proposed demonstration.
The historical calibration item's exact coverage cannot be checked because it was not supplied independently.

brief.title: Launching useful cargo into orbit with a beam
possible: People could send useful cargo into Earth orbit on a vehicle that receives most of its propulsion energy from a distant laser or microwave beam. The vehicle would turn that incoming energy into thrust throughout enough of its climb to reach orbit.
why: Launch vehicles could leave their main energy source on the ground or elsewhere in space. For launch designers, this would open a different way to power the climb and could reduce the energy supply carried aboard.

sources.showed: This paper reports a short laser-powered flight by a small Lightcraft vehicle.
sources.cited_for: It supports the case that a remote laser can propel a vehicle in flight.
sources.not_established: A short flight does not establish sustained beam-powered propulsion into orbit.

sources.who: DARPA and collaborators, with a receiver designed by Teravec Technologies
sources.showed: The team transmitted laser energy between ground stations and converted it into usable electricity.
sources.quote: Over the course of the test campaign, more than a megajoule of energy was transferred.
sources.cited_for: It demonstrates remote energy delivery and conversion into electricity.
sources.not_established: It does not establish propulsion, beam tracking during flight, or energy delivery throughout a climb to orbit.

shown: Lightcraft researchers reported a laser-powered vehicle reaching 71 metres. That demonstrates a short flight powered from a distance.
DARPA's team delivered more than 800 watts of usable power through a laser beam. Both ends stayed on the ground, so this demonstrated power transfer rather than flight.
missing: An integrated vehicle must receive enough beam energy for long enough to carry useful cargo into orbit.
The beam must stay aligned with a rapidly moving vehicle as distance, viewing angle and atmospheric conditions change.
The vehicle must turn received energy into enough thrust while surviving concentrated heating.

milestones.label: An independently measured orbit carrying at least 1 kilogram
milestones.explanation: Independent measurements would have to confirm the payload mass and an orbit lasting for a duration defined before launch. This would establish that useful cargo reached orbit.

milestones.label: The beam supplies most of the climb's propulsion energy
milestones.explanation: Measurements would have to show that the beam supplies more than half the propulsion energy during a predefined climb interval, accounting for losses and onboard energy. This would establish the beam as the main energy source.

milestones.label: Repeatable launches with independently assessable measurements
milestones.explanation: Repeated launches would have to provide independently assessable flight and energy measurements, with operating limits reported. This would establish repeatability within the tested conditions.

uncertain: The current altitude reached by beam-powered vehicles, and whether any have reached space or orbit, remain unresolved.
The energy measure must distinguish energy received from energy actually contributing to propulsion.
The required orbital lifetime, number of repeat launches and range of operating conditions still need to be defined.

page.title: Beamed-energy orbital launch
page.definition: A remote laser or microwave beam powers a vehicle’s ascent propulsion to place a 1 kg satellite in Earth orbit. The vehicle converts received radiation into thrust and may carry reaction mass, the material expelled to produce thrust.

goal.need: Liquid-oxygen/liquid-hydrogen engines provide about 450 s vacuum specific impulse, the effective exhaust speed divided by standard gravity. NASA Ames examined externally heated hydrogen at 2200 K for about 800 s. This motivates separating the propulsion energy source from the vehicle and its propellant; the beamed figure is a design estimate.

figures.caption: Specific impulse comparison in NASA Ames’s millimetre-wave thermal launch study.
figures.note: The beamed value is not a measured orbital-launch result.

statements.quote: The attraction of beamed-energy propulsion (BEP) is the potential for high specific impulse while removing the power-generation mass.

statements.body: Air Force Research Laboratory and NASA Marshall Space Flight Center, Lightcraft Technology Demonstrator programme
statements.quote: the advantage of leaving the propulsion energy source behind.
statements.context: The programme’s co-managers describe the motivation for beamed-energy propulsion.

statements.quote: to launch the first kilogram-class commercial micro-satellite with a megawatt ground-based infrared electric laser.

completion.title: A beam-powered launcher places a 1 kg satellite in low Earth orbit.
completion.criterion: An actual launch places a 1 kg satellite into low Earth orbit using a remote electromagnetic beam to power ascent propulsion. The Lightcraft programme specified laser propulsion; its satellite mass and orbital destination are the comparison target for the microwave case. The published target supplies no quantitative beam-energy-share, minimum orbital lifetime, or repeat-launch requirement.
completion.set_by: The AFRL/NASA Lightcraft Technology Demonstrator programme, described by its co-managers in Optics & Photonics News, January 1999. The published target concerns laser propulsion.
completion.threshold_quote: to launch a 1-kg nanosatellite into LEO
completion.basis: The programme’s co-managers identify delivery of a 1 kg satellite to low Earth orbit as the launch objective. This supplies an externally published payload and destination without adding an orbital lifetime or repetition count. Lightcraft Technologies subsequently stated a kilogram-class commercial satellite objective.

milestones.title: A beam-powered launch engine demonstrates predicted thrust generation in laboratory experiments.
milestones.criterion: Laboratory experiments support analytical predictions of conversion from beam energy to thrust, NASA’s TRL 3 test. Laser: one 23 cm engine tested from 9 July 1999 to 11 July 1999 produced up to 460 N/MW with pulse energies up to 667 J and 30 µs duration; the test count is unspecified. Microwave: a paper published on 20 May 2025 reports positive impulse at 28 GHz, 100–210 kW and 0.6–2.5 ms, with five repeats per condition. These component results are not formal readiness ratings of orbital launch systems.
milestones.set_by: NASA, NPR 7123.1D, Appendix E, TRL 3. This is a general hardware maturity criterion.
milestones.threshold_quote: Analytical and experimental proof-of-concept of critical function and/or characteristics.

milestones.title: A beam-powered launch vehicle lifts off under remotely supplied propulsion energy.
milestones.criterion: A model launch vehicle rises under thrust generated from remotely beamed energy. Laser: on 2 October 2000, a 50.62 g vehicle reached 71.1 m; the campaign comprised seven flights with three vehicles. Microwave: a paper published on 25 June 2025 analysed 14 launches of a 539 g model using a 170 GHz, 550 kW source; maximum rise was approximately 0.5 m with 43 pulses at 100 Hz. The microwave model was initially suspended by a string.
milestones.set_by: DARPA’s Millimeter-Wave Thermal Launch System challenge, initiated in 2012 and described by the project team in 2014. The original target concerns microwave thermal propulsion.
milestones.threshold_quote: launch a small thermal rocket into the air using millimeter waves.

milestones.title: A beam-powered launch vehicle reaches 30 km altitude on a suborbital trajectory.
milestones.criterion: Remote-beam propulsion takes a launch vehicle to 30 km altitude on a suborbital trajectory, one that returns to Earth without entering orbit. AFRL’s Phase II laser implementation specified a 100 kW pulsed carbon-dioxide laser.
milestones.set_by: Air Force Research Laboratory, Lightcraft Technology Demonstration programme, Phase II, as documented in AFRL-RZ-ED-TR-2007-0078. The published power and laser specification concern the laser case.
milestones.threshold_quote: to 30 km with a 100 kW pulsed CO2 laser.

milestones.title: A functional beam-powered launch vehicle flies beyond 100 km altitude.
milestones.criterion: A functioning beam-propelled vehicle makes a suborbital flight beyond 100 km altitude. AFRL’s Phase III called for a functional Lightcraft reaching space. FAI’s astronautical-flight boundary supplies the 100 km convention; AFRL did not specify that numerical boundary.
milestones.set_by: AFRL Lightcraft programme, Phase III, for a functional vehicle reaching space; Fédération Aéronautique Internationale, astronautical-flight boundary, for exceeding 100 km. AFRL’s vehicle target was laser-specific.
milestones.threshold_quote: when that flight goes beyond the 100 Km line, i.e. the Karman Line.

milestones.title: A complete beamed-energy orbital launch system qualifies for flight under NASA’s TRL 8 criterion.
milestones.criterion: The final launch-system configuration is completed and demonstrated through test and analysis for its intended operational environment and platform, with life testing where necessary. This applies NASA’s TRL 8 hardware criterion to the complete beamed-energy launch system, including the transmitter, beam control and vehicle, before the orbital demonstration.
milestones.set_by: NASA, NPR 7123.1D, Appendix E, TRL 8. This is a general hardware qualification criterion, not a published qualification of a beamed-energy launcher.
milestones.threshold_quote: Actual system completed and "flight qualified" through test and demonstration.

not_found: No published laser or microwave result was found for a 30 km launch, flight beyond 100 km, qualification of a complete orbital beamed-energy launcher, or delivery of a 1 kg satellite to orbit through 14 November 2026.
No programme acceptance protocol specifying beam-energy accounting, minimum orbital lifetime or repeat-launch count was found.
No authoritative current free-flight altitude record covering both beam types was found.
The full NASA/TM-2012-217014 PDF exceeded the retrieval limit; its NTRS abstract was accessible.
